docs.title: ruby_llm-providers-lms
docs.text:
A RubyLLM provider for LM Studio: run local models through the same Ruby API you use for hosted ones.

gem 'ruby_llm-providers-lms', require: 'ruby_llm/providers/lms'

chat = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)
chat.ask('Hello').content

No API key and no configuration: start LM Studio's server (lms server start) and the :lms provider talks to http://localhost:1234/v1.

Get started Judgments GitHub

docs.title: What it covers
docs.text:
LM Studio serves several APIs on one port, and this gem speaks all of them:

API What you get Protocols OpenAI Chat, streaming, tools, structured output, vision, reasoning, embeddings :chat_completions (default), :responses Anthropic Claude-style Messages API against a local model :anthropic Native REST Inference stats, server-stored conversations, MCP integrations, model management :native_v0, :native_chat Decisions Typed judgments from decision models: probabilities, choices and scores in milliseconds :decisions (default), :system_one

docs.title: New in 0.3: judgments with decision models
docs.text:
LM Studio 0.4.26 added endpoints for decision models: models that answer typed questions with probabilities instead of writing text. RubyLLM 2.1 calls these judgments, and this gem points them at LM Studio:

class TicketTriage < RubyLLM::Judge
  model 'd1-omni-600m', provider: :lms

  probability :urgent, 'Does this need attention today?'
  choice :team, 'Which team should handle this?' do
    billing   'Charges and refunds'
    technical 'Bugs and outages'
  end
  score :frustration, 'How frustrated is the customer?', %w[Calm Annoyed Angry]
end

judgment = TicketTriage.judge('You charged my card twice. Refund it today.')
judgment.urgent.probability  # => 0.97
judgment.team.choice         # => :billing

Open-source decision models such as D1 Omni 600M answer in tens of milliseconds on a laptop. See Judgments.

docs.title: The one thing to know first
docs.text:
What a call does depends on two choices, not one

LM Studio runs whatever model you downloaded behind every protocol. The protocol decides what is expressible — with_schema is honored on :chat_completions and silently ignored on :responses. The model decides whether it honors what the protocol accepted — qwen3 obeys tool_choice: "required", gpt-oss ignores it. Test against the models you intend to ship on. Choosing a protocol maps the first axis.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Ruby 3.3 or newer
  • RubyLLM 2.1.1 or newer
  • LM Studio with its server running (0.4.26 or newer for judgments)

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Most of what you call is RubyLLM's own API — RubyLLM.chat, RubyLLM.embed, RubyLLM.judge, RubyLLM::Judge — with provider: :lms. This page lists what the gem adds on top. RubyLLM's API is documented at rubyllm.com.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
require 'ruby_llm/providers/lms'

Registers the provider as :lms, with the packaged models.json as its model registry.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Situation Raised Server not running RubyLLM::Error — "Cannot connect to the LM Studio server at …. Start it with lms server start." Unknown model, or a chat model asked for a judgment RubyLLM::BadRequestError with LM Studio's message A decision response missing an answer RubyLLM::Error — "LM Studio Decisions returned an invalid judgment" A non-image attachment on a judgment RubyLLM::UnsupportedAttachmentError with_tools or with_schema on :native_chat RubyLLM::Error naming :chat_completions as the alternative, before any request is sent

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The gem is a single RubyLLM provider class, RubyLLM::Providers::LMS, with one protocol class per LM Studio dialect. RubyLLM does the rest: chats, streaming, tools, embeddings and judgments all run through RubyLLM's own machinery, and the provider decides which LM Studio endpoint each one reaches.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
RubyLLM asks the provider to resolve a protocol for every operation. The provider answers by operation, not just by configuration:

Operation Goes to Chosen by chat (ask, streaming, tools) the chat protocol lms_protocol, default :chat_completions embed :chat_completions → POST /v1/embeddings always — LM Studio serves embeddings nowhere else judge :decisions or :system_one lms_judgment_protocol, default :decisions list models :chat_completions, enriched from the native listing always — RubyLLM lists through the provider's default protocol, whatever lms_protocol says load / unload / download the provider's own ModelManagement methods —

The judgment route is the provider's private resolve_protocol override: when RubyLLM resolves with operation: :judge, it substitutes lms_judgment_protocol. Without it, lms_protocol = :anthropic would send judgments to a protocol that has none.

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text:
File Responsibility lib/ruby_llm/providers/lms.rb The provider: protocol registry, API base and auth headers, embedding and judgment routing, configuration options; registers :lms with RubyLLM at load time lms/connection_guard.rb Wraps RubyLLM's connection so a refused connection raises a RubyLLM::Error telling you to run lms server start lms/models.rb Model listing: OpenAI /v1/models enriched with native details; capabilities, modalities and metadata lms/native_v1.rb Rewrites the native v1 listing into the shape models.rb reads, including reasoning options and decision fields lms/endpoints.rb Native listing paths, spelled relative to the /v1 base lms/responses.rb :responses — reads LM Studio's reasoning_text as well as OpenAI's summaries lms/anthropic_messages.rb :anthropic — RubyLLM's Anthropic protocol with LM Studio's path lms/native_chat.rb, native_chat/* :native_chat — stateful /api/v1/chat, with conversation continuation and streaming lms/decisions.rb :decisions — OpenAI Decisions, answers matched to questions by name lms/system_one.rb :system_one — System One with the /v1-relative path and image support lms/model_management.rb native_models, loaded_models, load_model, unload_model, download_model lms/version.rb RubyLLM::Providers::LMS::VERSION

:chat_completions and :native_v0 are small classes defined in lms.rb itself; :native_v0 is the Chat Completions protocol pointed at /api/v0/chat/completions.

docs.title: Design rules
docs.text:
• Everything lives in RubyLLM::Providers::LMS. The gem adds no top-level constants. Archspec.rb enforces this, and that nothing under lib/ references RSpec, WebMock or VCR.
  • Subclass RubyLLM, don't fork it. Each protocol is RubyLLM's stock protocol with the smallest override LM Studio needs — a path, a response field, a matching rule.
  • Local means no ceremony. configuration_requirements is empty, so RubyLLM asks for no API key; local? is true, so it assumes any model id exists; the auth header is sent only when lms_api_key is set.
  • Paths are relative to the /v1 base. Native endpoints are reached as ../api/v1/... so a non-default lms_api_base moves everything together.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
bundle install
bundle exec rake              # rubocop, flay, archspec, specs
bundle exec rspec spec/ruby_llm/chat_spec.rb   # one file
bin/console                   # IRB with the gem loaded

Overcommit runs RuboCop, flay, archspec, RSpec and gitleaks as pre-commit hooks, so the full suite must pass before a commit lands.

docs.title: Tested against
docs.text:
Component Version LM Studio (macOS) 0.4.24+1 for the chat, embedding and model specs; 0.4.26 for judgments RubyLLM 2.1.1 (chat cassettes recorded on 2.0.0) Decision models kev-0.8b, d1-omni-600m, clef-flash (GGUF)

LM Studio's OpenAI-compatible surface is stable, but its native REST APIs (/api/v0, /api/v1) and the decision endpoints still change between releases. Check your own lms --version and the LM Studio release notes before assuming an endpoint behaves exactly as documented here.

docs.title: Specs
docs.text:
Two kinds:

  • spec/ruby_llm/providers/lms_spec.rb and most of spec/ruby_llm/providers/lms/ — unit specs for the provider: registration, protocols, configuration, listing, routing, judgment rendering and parsing. The two *_live_spec.rb files there are :live and record cassettes like the contract specs.
  • spec/ruby_llm/*_spec.rb — contract specs adapted from RubyLLM's live specs, tagged :live and driven by the model matrices in spec/support/models.rb.

docs.title: VCR cassettes
docs.text:
The first local run of a :live example calls the real LM Studio server and records a cassette in spec/fixtures/vcr_cassettes/; later runs replay it. CI (CI=1) only replays committed cassettes, so commit them.

A failing example keeps its cassette, so a red suite stays red. To re-record deliberately — after a behavior change or an LM Studio upgrade — run with RERECORD=1, which deletes the cassette of any example that fails so the next run records it fresh:

RERECORD=1 bundle exec rspec spec/ruby_llm/judgment_spec.rb

Cassette URIs are normalized to http://localhost:1234/v1, and VCR filters LMS_API_BASE and LMS_API_KEY out, so cassettes replay anywhere.

docs.title: Model matrices
docs.text:
Model ids are machine-specific. Put ids from lms ls into spec/support/models.rb before recording:

Matrix Needs CHAT_MODELS, TOOL_MODELS anything LM Studio serves TOOL_CHOICE_MODELS a model that obeys tool_choice: "required" (gpt-oss does not) STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_MODELS a model that does not mangle json_schema values (gpt-oss does) REASONING_MODELS a model whose listing reports reasoning options REASONING_OFF_MODELS one of those that also reports LM Studio's off VISION_MODELS a model flagged vision: true EMBEDDING_MODELS an embedding model NATIVE_CHAT_MODELS, MANAGEMENT_MODEL small models, so load/unload cycles stay fast NATIVE_REASONING_MODELS a model that emits reasoning items on the native endpoint (gpt-oss does; most instruct fine-tunes do not) JUDGMENT_MODELS decision models LM Studio tags type: "decision"; add vision: true for ones with a vision adapter

Matrices for operations LM Studio doesn't support (image generation, speech, video, moderation, rerank) are empty, which skips those files.

docs.title: The packaged catalog
docs.text: bundle exec rake models rewrites the sample models.json from your running server. It is a maintainer task for refreshing the shipped sample — see The Packaged Catalog.

docs.title: Architecture checks
docs.text: bundle exec rake archspec enforces the rules in Archspec.rb: everything under lib/ stays in the RubyLLM::Providers::LMS namespace and never references RSpec, WebMock or VCR. bundle exec rake flay flags duplicated code above a mass of 70.

docs.text: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs bundle exec rake on Ruby 3.3, 3.4 and 4.0. The committed Gemfile.lock must install on every one of them.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Twenty runnable scripts live in examples/. Start LM Studio's server, then run any of them from the repo root:

lms server start
ruby examples/01_basic_usage.rb
ruby examples/run_all.rb        # every numbered demo, in order, with a banner each

examples/common.rb holds the shared setup: it configures RubyLLM from the environment (a .env file is honored) and defines the default models.

Variable Default Used by LMS_API_BASE http://localhost:1234/v1 all LMS_API_KEY none all, only for a server behind auth LMS_MODEL qwen/qwen3.8-27b the chat demos, the chat-model check in 18, and the replies in 20 LMS_EMBEDDING_MODEL text-embedding-nomic-embed-text-v1.5 05 LMS_REASONING_MODEL openai/gpt-oss-20b 13 LMS_DECISION_MODEL d1-omni-600m 16-20

Model ids are machine-specific: use ones lms ls shows on your machine.

docs.text:

LMS_DECISION_MODEL=clef-flash ruby examples/17_judge_class.rb   # try another model

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Three short steps from nothing to a local model answering in Ruby:

  1. Installation — LM Studio, a model, and the gem.
  2. Quick Start — a chat, a stream, an embedding and a judgment.
  3. Configuration — the four settings, all optional.

Once those work, Choosing a Protocol explains the dialects LM Studio speaks, and Judgments covers the decision-model endpoints.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is optional. The provider has four settings, all on RubyLLM's configuration object:

Option Default Purpose lms_api_base http://localhost:1234/v1 Where the server is, ending in /v1 like the default; the native (/api/...) and decision paths are worked out relative to it. lms_api_key nil Sent as a bearer token only when set — for a server behind an auth proxy. lms_protocol :chat_completions Which dialect chats use. See Choosing a Protocol. lms_judgment_protocol :decisions Which endpoint judgments use. See Choosing the Endpoint. 
require 'ruby_llm/providers/lms'

RubyLLM.configure do |config|
  config.lms_api_base = ENV.fetch('LMS_API_BASE', 'http://localhost:1234/v1')
  config.lms_api_key = ENV['LMS_API_KEY'] # only if your server requires auth
end

docs.title: Scoping a setting
docs.text:
The protocol options can be set process-wide, for one block of work, or for a single chat:

RubyLLM.configure { |config| config.lms_protocol = :anthropic }   # process-wide

RubyLLM.context { |config| config.lms_protocol = :native_v0 }     # one context
       .chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)

RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms,              # one chat
             protocol: :native_chat, assume_model_exists: true)

Judgments scope the same way through a context:

context = RubyLLM.context { |config| config.lms_judgment_protocol = :system_one }
RubyLLM.judge('...', questions: { ... }, model: 'd1-omni-600m', provider: :lms, context:)

docs.title: The two protocol settings are independent
docs.text:
lms_protocol never affects embeddings or judgments:

  • Embeddings always go to POST /v1/embeddings, the only place LM Studio serves them — even when lms_protocol is :anthropic.
  • Judgments always go to a decision endpoint, chosen by lms_judgment_protocol. A chat protocol never handles them.

docs.title: A default judgment model
docs.text:
RubyLLM's default_judgment_model setting applies when a judgment names no model. Set it to a decision model you have downloaded so RubyLLM.judge and judge classes without a model line work:

RubyLLM.configure do |config|
  config.default_judgment_model = 'd1-omni-600m'
end

Pass provider: :lms on the call (or in the judge class's model line) so RubyLLM routes it to this provider.

docs.title: Environment variables in the examples
docs.text: The scripts in examples/ read LMS_API_BASE, LMS_API_KEY, LMS_MODEL, LMS_EMBEDDING_MODEL, LMS_REASONING_MODEL and LMS_DECISION_MODEL (a .env file in the repo root is honored). The gem itself reads no environment variables.

docs.title: 1. LM Studio and its server
docs.text:
Install LM Studio, then start its local server, either from the app's Developer tab or with the lms CLI:

lms server start

The server listens on http://localhost:1234 by default. If it isn't running, every request from this gem raises a RubyLLM::Error that tells you to start it, rather than a raw connection failure.

docs.title: 2. A model
docs.text:
The gem talks to whatever models you have downloaded. Get one from the app's search, or with lms get:

lms get qwen/qwen3-4b                                    # a chat model
lms get https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/d1-omni-600M-GGUF  # a decision model, for judgments
lms ls                                                   # what you have

Use the identifiers lms ls shows (qwen/qwen3-4b, d1-omni-600m) as model ids in Ruby — not OpenAI model names.

docs.title: 3. The gem
docs.text:
Add it to your Gemfile:

gem 'ruby_llm-providers-lms', require: 'ruby_llm/providers/lms'

and bundle install. Requiring ruby_llm/providers/lms registers the :lms provider with RubyLLM; there is nothing else to set up.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Component Version Ruby 3.3 or newer (CI runs 3.3, 3.4 and 4.0) RubyLLM 2.1.1 or newer LM Studio any recent build; 0.4.26 or newer for judgments

See Development for the exact versions the documentation was checked against.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Every snippet below assumes LM Studio's server is running and the model named is downloaded.

require 'ruby_llm/providers/lms'

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
chat = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)
response = chat.ask('Hello')
response.content          # => "Hello! How can I help you today?"
chat.ask('What did I just say?')  # multi-turn context, as with any provider

Because LM Studio is a local provider, RubyLLM assumes any model id you pass exists — it needs no entry in the model registry and no assume_model_exists: — and LM Studio just-in-time loads the model if it isn't loaded yet. Expect the first request to a cold model to take a while.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: chat.ask('Write a haiku about Ruby') { |chunk| print chunk.content }

docs.title: Tools and structured output
docs.text:
Everything RubyLLM can express works on the default protocol:

class Weather < RubyLLM::Tool
  description 'Current weather for a city'
  parameter :city, description: 'City name'

  def execute(city:) = { city:, forecast: 'sunny', celsius: 21 }
end

RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)
       .with_tools(Weather).ask('What is the weather in Paris?')

schema = { type: 'object', properties: { name: { type: 'string' }, age: { type: 'integer' } },
           required: %w[name age] }
response = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)
                  .with_schema(schema).ask('John is 30 years old.')
response.content  # => "{\"name\": \"John\", \"age\": 30}"
response.parsed   # => {"name" => "John", "age" => 30}

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text: RubyLLM.embed('Hello world', model: 'text-embedding-nomic-embed-text-v1.5', provider: :lms)

docs.title: A judgment
docs.text:
With a decision model downloaded, ask typed questions and get numbers back:

judgment = RubyLLM.judge(
  'The blender arrived late, but it works perfectly. Best purchase this year.',
  questions: {
    satisfied: { type: :probability, instructions: 'Is the customer satisfied with the product?' },
    topic: { type: :choice, instructions: 'What is the review mostly about?',
             options: { shipping: 'Delivery', quality: 'How well it works' } }
  },
  model: 'd1-omni-600m', provider: :lms
)

judgment.satisfied.probability  # => 0.964
judgment.topic.choice           # => :quality

docs.title: What's on the server
docs.text:
provider = RubyLLM::Provider.resolve!(:lms).new(RubyLLM.config)
provider.list_models.each { |model| puts "#{model.id}  #{model.capabilities.join(', ')}" }

docs.title: Judgments
docs.text:
LM Studio 0.4.26 added two endpoints for decision models: models that answer typed questions with probabilities instead of generating text. RubyLLM 2.1 calls this a judgment (RubyLLM.judge, RubyLLM::Judge), and this gem points judgments at LM Studio.

A decision model reads the input once and answers every question with numbers. There is no output to parse and no format to coax, and it writes nothing — so it answers in milliseconds. On an M2 Max, D1 Omni 600M answers three questions about a support ticket in about 30 ms.

docs.title: Three kinds of question
docs.text:
Type Ask it with Answer object What you read probability probability :name, 'question?' RubyLLM::Probability probability — the chance the answer is yes, 0 to 1 choice choice :name, 'question?' do ... end RubyLLM::Choice choice (a Symbol), probabilities per option, confidence score score :name, 'question?', levels RubyLLM::Score score (can fall between levels), levels, probabilities per level index, confidence

One call can ask any number of questions; they all ride in a single request.

docs.title: Ad hoc: RubyLLM.judge
docs.text:
review = <<~TEXT
  The blender arrived two days late, which was annoying. But it crushes ice in
  seconds, it is quiet, and smoothies come out perfectly smooth. Best kitchen
  purchase this year.
TEXT

judgment = RubyLLM.judge(
  review,
  questions: {
    satisfied: { type: :probability, instructions: 'Is the customer satisfied with the product?' },
    topic: { type: :choice, instructions: 'What is the review mostly about?',
             options: { shipping: 'Delivery speed or damage in transit', quality: 'How well the product works',
                        support: 'Dealing with customer service', price: 'Cost or value for money' } },
    sentiment: { type: :score, instructions: 'Overall, how does the customer feel about the product?',
                 levels: %w[Furious Unhappy Mixed Happy Delighted] }
  },
  model: 'd1-omni-600m', provider: :lms
)

judgment.satisfied.probability    # => 0.997
judgment.topic.choice             # => :quality
judgment.topic.probabilities      # => {shipping: 0.007, quality: 0.891, support: 0.011, price: 0.09}
judgment.sentiment.score          # => 3.95
judgment.sentiment.levels[judgment.sentiment.score.round]  # => "Delighted"

Numbers are model- and wording-specific

Every figure on these pages came from a real run on the author's machine. Small decision models are sensitive to phrasing: shorten that review to one sentence and D1 Omni 600M's satisfied drops from 0.997 to 0.18, while Clef Flash barely moves. See Patterns and Tuning.

Question hashes take type:, instructions:, and the type's criteria key: criteria: (yes/no descriptions) for a probability, options: for a choice, levels: for a score.

docs.title: Reusable: a RubyLLM::Judge subclass
docs.text:
Declare the questions once and run the judge over every record:

class TicketTriage < RubyLLM::Judge
  model 'd1-omni-600m', provider: :lms

  inputs :teams  # supplied per call; read by the lambda below

  probability :urgent, 'Does this need attention today?'
  choice :team, 'Which team should handle this?', -> { teams }
  score :frustration, 'How frustrated is the customer?', %w[Calm Annoyed Frustrated Angry]
end

judgment = TicketTriage.judge('The API has returned 500 errors for an hour!',
                              teams: { billing: 'Charges and refunds', technical: 'Bugs and outages' })
judgment.team.choice  # => :technical

RubyLLM's judgments guide covers the whole DSL: structured (Hash) input, blocks, dynamic options and provider options.

docs.title: What a judgment carries
docs.text:
Method Returns judgment.<name> / judgment[:name] / judgment.fetch(:name) the answer for one question judgment.each { \|name, answer\| } every answer, in question order judgment.model the instance that answered (d1-omni-600m, or clef-flash:2 for a second instance) judgment.tokens input tokens; output is always 0 judgment.to_h model, answers, tokens and cost as plain data judgment.raw the HTTP response from LM Studio

Judgments are instrumented as judgment.ruby_llm events, like chats.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• You need LM Studio 0.4.26 or newer and a model LM Studio recognizes as a decision model. A chat model is refused. See Decision Models.
  • Two endpoints serve judgments; the default is fine to start with. See Choosing the Endpoint — the choice matters more for small models than you might expect.
  • Models with a vision adapter judge images too: Judging Images.
  • Wording and thresholds are where the work is: Patterns and Tuning.

docs.title: Decision Models
docs.text: A judgment needs a decision model: a model built to score typed questions rather than generate text. Open-source ones are published as GGUF files on Hugging Face, and LM Studio runs the GGUF builds.

docs.title: Models known to work
docs.text:
These three were verified end to end with this gem, over both decision endpoints:

Model Hugging Face Params Size Images decision_type License D1 Omni 600M LiquidAI/d1-omni-600M-GGUF 600M 0.8 GB yes lfm2-d1-omni Liquid AI's own license Kev 0.8B ggml-org/Kev-0.8B-GGUF 753M 0.8 GB no kev Apache-2.0 Clef Flash ggml-org/Clef-Flash-GGUF 9.1B 7.4 GB yes clef Apache-2.0

Download with lms get and the repository URL:

lms get https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/d1-omni-600M-GGUF
lms get https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Kev-0.8B-GGUF
lms get https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Clef-Flash-GGUF

lms ls then lists them under their own DECISION heading.

Other repositories tagged decision-model on Hugging Face — the rest of the ggml-org Kev, Clef and vllm-d3 families, Laya, Julia-1, LiquidAI's d1-3B — should work too, as long as LM Studio lists them as decision models. Check each license: some (OpenJev, Bespoke-Nimble) are non-commercial.

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
Measured on an M2 Max with the questions from example 18_decision_models.rb (one ticket, three questions), warm model:

Model Time per judgment Quality, in practice D1 Omni 600M ~30 ms Strong on clear-cut text and spam; noticeably sensitive to wording; reads images reliably only over :system_one Kev 0.8B ~65 ms Least sure of itself; sent "I was charged twice. Please fix it today." to other rather than billing, and could not spot a gift-card scam Clef Flash ~600 ms Most accurate and most consistent across wording and endpoints; reads images over both endpoints

A reasonable default: start with D1 Omni 600M, tune your questions on it, and move to Clef Flash where the small model's answers aren't trustworthy enough. Examples 16-20 default to D1 Omni 600M (LMS_DECISION_MODEL overrides it).

docs.title: It has to be a decision model to LM Studio
docs.text:
LM Studio decides what counts, and it must say so itself. GET /api/v1/models reports a recognized model with type: "decision":

{ "key": "d1-omni-600m", "type": "decision", "decision_type": "lfm2-d1-omni",
  "has_vision_adapter": true, "architecture": "lfm2", "format": "gguf" }

A model that merely shares a decision model's name is not enough. An MLX conversion of Clef Flash (mlx-community/clef-flash) loads as an ordinary LLM, and both decision endpoints reject it. Use the GGUF repositories above.

A chat model is refused with a RubyLLM::BadRequestError:

Invalid model identifier "qwen/qwen3.8-27b". Please specify a valid downloaded
model (e.g., d1-omni-600m, kev-0.8b, clef-flash).

With no decision model downloaded at all, the message is "There are no downloaded decision models."

docs.title: How the gem lists them
docs.text:
provider.list_models reports decision models as judgment models, so you can find them programmatically:

provider = RubyLLM::Provider.resolve!(:lms).new(RubyLLM.config)
deciders = provider.list_models.select { |model| model.capabilities.include?('judgment') }

deciders.each do |model|
  puts [model.id, model.metadata[:decision_type], model.modalities.input.inspect].join('  ')
end
# clef-flash    clef          ["text", "image"]
# d1-omni-600m  lfm2-d1-omni  ["text", "image"]
# kev-0.8b      kev           ["text"]
Field For a decision model capabilities ["judgment"] and nothing else — they don't chat modalities.output ["judgment"] modalities.input ["text"], plus "image" when LM Studio reports a vision adapter metadata[:decision_type] the kind of decision model, as LM Studio reports it

docs.title: Loading and memory
docs.text: Decision models load on demand like any other model, with the same idle TTL. One quirk worth knowing: if you load a model yourself (in the app, or with lms load) and a decision request then loads it on demand, LM Studio can start a second instance beside yours. lms ps shows both (clef-flash and clef-flash:2), each holding its own memory, and judgment.model reports the instance that answered — clef-flash:2, not the model id. Unload the copy you don't need with lms unload.

docs.title: Choosing the Endpoint
docs.text:
LM Studio serves decision models through two endpoints, and the gem has a protocol for each:

:decisions (default) :system_one Endpoint POST /v1/decisions POST /v1/systemone Origin OpenAI's Decisions API Jev (TypeSafe) System One API Input field input state (required) Questions an array: {type: predicate \| choice \| score, name, instructions, choices \| levels} a hash keyed by name: {type: noul \| choice \| score, instructions, criteria} Probability criteria folded into the instruction text as "Yes: … / No: …" lines sent as structured criteria Images input_image data URLs inside a content array data URLs in a top-level images array Answers an array with a name on each a hash keyed by question name

Pick one with lms_judgment_protocol:

RubyLLM.configure { |config| config.lms_judgment_protocol = :system_one }  # process-wide

context = RubyLLM.context { |config| config.lms_judgment_protocol = :system_one }
RubyLLM.judge(text, questions: { ... }, model: 'd1-omni-600m', provider: :lms, context:)

Judgments go to a decision endpoint whatever lms_protocol says; a chat protocol never handles them.

docs.title: Do the answers differ?
docs.text:
For a large model, barely. For a small one, sometimes a lot. The two endpoints phrase the same questions to the model differently, and a 600M-parameter model notices. From example 18_decision_models.rb, one billing ticket:

Model Endpoint Urgent Team Confidence Mood (0..2) Clef Flash decisions 0.96 billing 0.96 1.21 Clef Flash system_one 0.95 billing 0.97 1.15 D1 Omni 600M decisions 0.91 billing 0.51 0.53 D1 Omni 600M system_one 0.91 billing 0.94 1.08 Kev 0.8B decisions 0.64 billing 0.66 1.03 Kev 0.8B system_one 0.64 billing 0.70 1.21

The biggest gap is probability criteria — the optional yes/no descriptions on a probability question. Decisions has no field for them, so RubyLLM folds them into the instruction text; System One sends them as data:

recommend: { type: :probability,
             instructions: 'Would this customer recommend the product to a friend?',
             criteria: { yes: 'Ends satisfied with the product itself', no: 'Would steer others away' } }
Model decisions system_one Clef Flash 0.758 0.910 D1 Omni 600M 0.012 0.803 Kev 0.8B 0.602 0.788

Same model, same question, opposite conclusions. Images show the same pattern for D1 Omni 600M.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
1. Pick the endpoint first. :decisions is the default and fine for most work; with D1 Omni 600M and either probability criteria or images, :system_one gave clearly better answers on the author's machine.
  2. Tune on that endpoint. Thresholds and wording tuned on one endpoint don't carry over to the other unchanged.
  3. Prefer guidance in the question text over criteria when you need to switch endpoints: the instruction text reaches the model the same way on both.

docs.title: Gem-specific details
docs.text:
• Answers are matched by name. RubyLLM 2.1.1's stock Decisions protocol pairs answers with questions by position; LM Studio returns them in question order today, but the gem matches on each answer's name so a reordering can't silently swap answers. A missing answer raises RubyLLM::Error.
  • The System One path is fixed for an lms_api_base that already ends in /v1 (the stock protocol would request /v1/v1/systemone).
  • System One images go in the top-level images array, where LM Studio reads them; the stock protocol refuses images entirely. See Judging Images.

docs.title: Judging Images
docs.text:
A decision model with a vision adapter answers questions about pictures. Pass them with with:, exactly as for a chat — a path, a URL, or several of either:

judgment = RubyLLM.judge(
  questions: {
    damaged: { type: :probability, instructions: 'Is the package damaged?' },
    color: { type: :choice, instructions: 'What color is the box?',
             options: { brown: nil, white: nil, other: nil } }
  },
  with: 'delivery_photo.jpg',
  model: 'clef-flash', provider: :lms
)

Text is optional when there is an image; pass it as the first argument to give the model context (RubyLLM.judge('Customer photo of the delivered box', with: 'box.png', ...)). A judge class takes with: the same way: TicketTriage.judge(ticket_text, with: screenshot).

docs.title: Which models
docs.text:
Only models LM Studio reports a vision adapter for — list_models shows image among their input modalities. Of the verified models, D1 Omni 600M and Clef Flash read images; Kev 0.8B does not, and LM Studio says so:

kev-0.8b: This server does not support image input for decisions. For a model
that supports it, start it with `--mmproj`

A non-image attachment such as a PDF raises RubyLLM::UnsupportedAttachmentError before any request is sent.

docs.title: How images travel
docs.text:
Both endpoints take images as inline base64 data URLs — RubyLLM reads the file and encodes it, and the gem puts it where each endpoint expects, so LM Studio never has to fetch anything:

Endpoint Where the image goes :decisions an input_image part in the input's content array, beside an input_text part when there is text :system_one a top-level images array; state carries the text, or "" when there is none (the endpoint requires it)

Why :system_one images needed the gem's help

LM Studio's docs say System One accepts "inline base64 data URLs" without naming the field, and RubyLLM's stock System One protocol refuses images. Testing found the top-level images array: a red image scores 0.98-0.996 on "Is the image red?" and a blue one 0.005-0.07. A Responses-style content array in state is accepted too, but its image is ignored — the answer doesn't change with the picture.

docs.title: Results on solid colors
docs.text:
From example 19_judging_images.rb — five solid swatches, "What color is the image?" with the five colors as options:

Image Clef Flash, decisions Clef Flash, system_one D1 Omni 600M, decisions D1 Omni 600M, system_one red red (0.85) red (0.98) blue (0.61) red (0.99) green green (0.94) green (0.98) green (0.99) green (1.00) blue blue (0.95) blue (0.98) blue (0.27) blue (0.84) black black (0.95) black (0.98) white (0.67) black (1.00) white white (0.94) white (0.97) white (0.87) white (0.85)

Clef Flash is right on both endpoints. D1 Omni 600M is right on every image over :system_one but miscalls two of five over :decisions, with or without text beside the image. The request the gem sends is a plain data URL in both cases; the difference is in how LM Studio presents the image to that model.

If you judge images with a small model, use :system_one, and check your own model on your own images before trusting it.

docs.title: Keep the policy in the judge, the decisions in Ruby
docs.text:
A judge class says what to ask. What to do with the answers belongs in plain Ruby, where thresholds are easy to test and change:

URGENT = 0.7
ANGRY = 2.0   # Frustrated or worse on a 0..3 scale
UNSURE = 0.5  # below this team confidence, a person should look

def route(judgment)
  return 'escalate to on-call lead' if judgment.urgent.probability >= URGENT && judgment.frustration.score >= ANGRY
  return 'human triage (team unclear)' if judgment.team.confidence < UNSURE
  return "#{judgment.team.choice} queue, priority" if judgment.urgent.probability >= URGENT

  "#{judgment.team.choice} queue"
end

Use confidence as a "don't know" signal: a choice with low confidence is a case for a human, not a coin flip. Example 17_judge_class.rb routes a small inbox this way.

docs.title: Screen with a decision model, write with a chat model
docs.text:
A decision model answers in tens of milliseconds and writes nothing; a chat model takes seconds to write a reply. Put the first in front of the second so the expensive model only sees what deserves it:

class ContactScreen < RubyLLM::Judge
  model 'd1-omni-600m', provider: :lms

  probability :spam, 'Is this message spam?'
  probability :needs_reply, 'Does this message need a response from our team?'
  choice :kind, 'What kind of message is this?' do
    question  'Asking how something works or whether we offer it'
    complaint 'Reporting a problem or unhappy with something'
    praise    'Saying thanks or something positive'
    other     'Anything else'
  end
end

inbox.each do |message|
  screen = ContactScreen.judge(message)
  next if screen.spam.probability >= 0.5 || screen.needs_reply.probability < 0.6

  RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3.8-27b', provider: :lms)
         .with_instructions("Reply briefly to this #{screen.kind.choice}.")
         .ask(message)
end

In example 20_judge_then_chat.rb, screening five messages took 160 ms and drafting the two that needed replies took about 49 s. Without the screen, the spam would have gone to the chat model too. The judgment's choice also rides into the prompt, so the chat model knows what it is answering.

docs.title: Wording matters more than you'd think
docs.text:
Small decision models are sensitive to phrasing. Measured while building the examples:

Question D1 Omni 600M Kev 0.8B Clef Flash "Would this customer recommend the product to a friend?" (glowing review with a late delivery) 0.22 0.90 0.95 "Is the customer satisfied with the product?" (same review) 0.98 0.89 0.97 "Is this message spam?" (gift-card scam) 0.95 0.29 0.95 "Is the sender asking a question or waiting for an answer from us?" (broken-item complaint) 0.26 — — "Does this message need a response from our team?" (same complaint) 0.80 0.65 0.95

The rows come from separate runs with different question batches, and a figure moves a little with what else is in the request: the "satisfied" question scored 0.98 on D1 Omni 600M here and 0.997 when batched with the questions on the Judgments page.

What worked:

  • Short, plain, direct questions. The wordier "Is this an unsolicited advertisement or scam rather than a real customer writing to us?" caught spam as well as "Is this message spam?", but it also rated a genuine "Do you ship to Canada?" as 0.52 spam on D1 Omni 600M, where the short question gave 0.02.
  • Ask about the thing itself. "Is the customer satisfied with the product?" rather than a hypothetical like "Would they recommend it?".
  • One condition per question. If "spam" and "unsolicited marketing" need different handling, ask them separately rather than in one question.

And always: test on the model and the endpoint you will deploy on. Criteria in particular can flip a small model's answer between endpoints.

docs.title: Batch the questions, not the requests
docs.text: Every question in a judge rides in the same request. Adding a question costs input tokens, not another round trip — ask everything you need in one judgment rather than calling once per question. judgment.tokens.input shows what a set of questions costs.

docs.title: A default model
docs.text:
Set RubyLLM's default_judgment_model to a decision model and judge classes can omit the model (still pass provider: :lms on the call):

RubyLLM.configure { |config| config.default_judgment_model = 'd1-omni-600m' }
RubyLLM.judge(text, questions: { ... }, provider: :lms)

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
LM Studio serves whatever models you have downloaded — chat models, embedding models and decision models — so the provider asks the server what it has rather than relying on a fixed list.

provider = RubyLLM::Provider.resolve!(:lms).new(RubyLLM.config)
provider.list_models.each { |model| puts "#{model.id}  #{model.capabilities.join(', ')}" }

You don't need a catalog to use a model: because :lms is a local provider, RubyLLM assumes any id you pass exists and LM Studio loads it on demand.

docs.title: What listing enrichment adds
docs.text:
list_models starts from the OpenAI-compatible /v1/models listing, which carries little beyond an id, and merges in LM Studio's native listing. It tries GET /api/v1/models first and falls back to GET /api/v0/models; when neither answers — an older build, or the native API turned off — the plain listing is still returned.

Model#name becomes the display name where one is reported ("Qwen3 27B" rather than "qwen/qwen3.8-27b"), and Model#metadata picks up whatever the server knows:

Key From Example owned_by the OpenAI listing "organization_owner" publisher, arch, quantization, compatibility_type, state v0 and v1 "qwen", "qwen35", "Q4_K_M", "gguf", "loaded" display_name, description v1 "Qwen3 27B" params_string, size_bytes, bits_per_weight v1 "27B", 17742039110, 4 variants, selected_variant v1 the downloaded quantizations, and which one is selected reasoning_options v1 [{type: "effort", values: ["none", "low", "medium", "xhigh"], default: "xhigh"}, {type: "toggle"}] loaded_context_length v1 8192 — the loaded instance's window, which can be smaller than context_window remaining_ttl_seconds v1 1050 — how long before an idle JIT-loaded instance evicts decision_type v1, decision models only "lfm2-d1-omni", "kev", "clef"

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Kind of model capabilities modalities Chat streaming, structured_output, plus function_calling and tool_choice (tool-trained), vision, reasoning as the listing reports text in (plus image for vision), text out Embedding none text in, embeddings out Decision judgment only text in (plus image with a vision adapter), judgment out

streaming and structured_output hold for every chat model LM Studio serves: the server constrains generation with a grammar built from your schema, so structured output works even on weights with no tool training — whether the values are any good is a separate question.

Decision models don't chat, so they get the judgment capability and output modality and nothing else. See Decision Models.

docs.title: Model lifecycle: JIT loading, TTL, auto-evict
docs.text:
The server manages memory rather than a fleet:

JIT loading With just-in-time loading enabled (the server default), /v1/models lists every downloaded model and a request for an unloaded model loads it on demand. Expect a long time to first token on that first request. With JIT off, only loaded models are served. TTL JIT-loaded models default to a 60-minute idle TTL. Override it per request with the ttl request extra, or at load time with lms load <model> --ttl 3600. Models loaded explicitly with lms load have no TTL and stay until unloaded. Auto-evict By default LM Studio keeps at most one JIT-loaded model in memory, evicting the previous one before loading the next. Turn auto-evict off in the server settings to keep several resident at once.

The state metadata (loaded / not-loaded) shows which models are resident right now; Model Management lets you change that from Ruby.

docs.title: The Packaged Catalog
docs.text:
The gem ships a models.json at its root, which RubyLLM loads as the provider's model registry so RubyLLM.models has something to show.

This file is only a sample

It was recorded from the author's machine. LM Studio serves whatever models you have downloaded, so your catalog will be different.

RubyLLM.models.refresh does not query your LM Studio server: provider gems that ship a registry file are excluded from the live fetch. Refresh still updates the remote providers, but for :lms it only re-reads the registered models.json. Your live server is still the source of truth, reached differently depending on what you need:

Chatting, embedding, judging Needs no catalog at all — any model id LM Studio knows works. Browsing what your server offers provider.list_models, which hits the live endpoints every time. Making RubyLLM.models reflect your machine

Register your own catalog file in place of the shipped sample:

require 'ruby_llm/providers/lms'

provider = RubyLLM::Provider.resolve!(:lms).new(RubyLLM.config)
RubyLLM::Models.new(provider.list_models).save_to_json('my_models.json')
RubyLLM::Provider.register :lms, RubyLLM::Providers::LMS, models: 'my_models.json'
RubyLLM.models.refresh

Some features read the registry rather than the server — notably reasoning, which uses each model's reasoning options to decide what with_thinking may ask for. Register your own catalog to get those right for your models.

Don't edit the models.json inside the installed gem — it is overwritten on every gem update.

For maintainers, bundle exec rake models regenerates the shipped sample from a running server; see Development.

docs.title: Model Management
docs.text:
The provider exposes LM Studio's native model-management endpoints, so you can control what is in memory without shelling out to lms:

provider = RubyLLM::Provider.resolve!(:lms).new(RubyLLM.config)

provider.native_models   # every downloaded model, with architecture,
                         # quantization, capabilities, loaded_instances, ...
provider.loaded_models   # just the ones resident in memory

instance = provider.load_model('qwen/qwen3-4b', context_length: 8192)
# => { "instance_id" => "qwen/qwen3-4b", "status" => "loaded", ... }
provider.unload_model(instance['instance_id'])

provider.download_model('qwen/qwen3-4b')  # fetch a new model onto disk
Method Endpoint Returns native_models GET /api/v1/models every downloaded model as LM Studio describes it, as an Array of Hashes loaded_models GET /api/v1/models the subset with at least one loaded instance load_model(model, context_length: nil, **options) POST /api/v1/models/load the server's response Hash, including instance_id unload_model(instance_id) POST /api/v1/models/unload the server's response Hash download_model(model, **options) POST /api/v1/models/download the server's response Hash

Extra keyword options go into the request as-is; the server rejects keys it doesn't know.

docs.title: Instances
docs.text:
load_model returns the instance_id that unload_model takes. Loading a model that is already resident starts a second instance (...:2), so hold on to the id you were given.

For the same reason these calls are sent non-idempotent: RubyLLM retries a POST that times out, and a retried load of a large model would hold the weights in memory twice.

The same thing can happen behind your back with decision models: a model you loaded yourself, then requested on demand by a judgment, can end up with two instances. See Decision Models.

docs.title: TTL
docs.text:
ttl is not a load option on the native API. Set idle TTL per request through the OpenAI endpoints (the ttl request extra) or with lms load --ttl.

Example 14_model_management.rb lists, loads and unloads a model.

docs.title: Choosing a Protocol
docs.text:
LM Studio speaks several APIs on one port, and runs whatever model you have downloaded behind all of them. This gem registers a protocol for each:

API Endpoints Protocols OpenAI POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /v1/responses, GET /v1/models, POST /v1/embeddings :chat_completions (default), :responses Anthropic POST /v1/messages :anthropic Native REST v0: POST /api/v0/chat/completions, GET /api/v0/models v1: POST /api/v1/chat, GET /api/v1/models, POST /api/v1/models/load, /unload, /download :native_v0, :native_chat Decisions POST /v1/decisions, POST /v1/systemone :decisions (default for judgments), :system_one

The first three APIs carry the five chat protocols, selected with lms_protocol. The decision protocols serve only judgments and are selected separately with lms_judgment_protocol — see Configuration.

docs.title: Two choices, not one
docs.text:
The protocol and the model each decide part of the outcome

The protocol decides what is expressible. with_schema is honored on :chat_completions and :native_v0 and silently ignored on :responses and :anthropic — same model, same schema, prose where you expected JSON. Reasoning is spelled none/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh on the OpenAI endpoints and off/low/medium/high/xhigh/on on the native one. That much is consistent for every model, and this gem papers over what it can.

The model decides whether it honors what the protocol accepted, and no provider code can fix that. LM Studio forwards tool_choice: "required" for anything — qwen3 obeys it, gpt-oss ignores it. It constrains generation with a grammar built from your schema, so every model returns structurally valid JSON — and gpt-oss returns {"name":"analysis","age":0}, which parses cleanly and means nothing.

This is the price of LM Studio's reach: it is all things to all models. Test against the models you actually intend to ship on, rather than assuming a capability carries across either axis.

docs.title: The chat protocols compared
docs.text:
Stay on the default unless you need something only another column offers.

:chat_completions :responses :anthropic :native_v0 :native_chat Streaming yes yes yes yes yes Client-side tools (with_tools) yes yes yes yes no — raises; use MCP integrations Structured output (with_schema) yes ignored, silently ignored, silently yes no — raises Inference stats no no no yes, via raw yes, via tokens LM Studio request extras yes yes yes yes sampling settings only — see Native REST API Server-stored conversations no no no no yes Reasoning control yes yes yes yes yes Reasoning text returned yes yes yes yes yes

Checked against LM Studio 0.4.24+1; the :anthropic reasoning rows and the decision endpoints against 0.4.26. The cells that say the server ignores something describe observed behavior, not anything the gem enforces.

Where a protocol ignores something silently rather than raising, its page says so — those are the cases that cost you an afternoon. Example 15_protocol_matrix.rb runs the with_schema row against your own models.

"Reasoning control" means with_thinking reaches the server. Whether a given model reasons at all is a separate question — see Reasoning.

docs.title: Selecting one
docs.text:
RubyLLM.configure { |config| config.lms_protocol = :anthropic }      # process-wide

RubyLLM.context { |config| config.lms_protocol = :native_v0 }        # one context
       .chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)

RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms,                 # one chat
             protocol: :native_chat, assume_model_exists: true)

Whatever lms_protocol says, embeddings go to /v1/embeddings and judgments go to a decision endpoint.

docs.title: The Anthropic API — :anthropic
docs.text:
LM Studio serves Anthropic's Messages API at POST /v1/messages, so a codebase written against Claude can point at a local model without changing how it talks:

RubyLLM.configure { |config| config.lms_protocol = :anthropic }

chat = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)
chat.ask('Hello').raw.body
# => {"id" => "msg_...", "type" => "message", "role" => "assistant",
#     "content" => [{"type" => "text", "text" => "..."}],
#     "stop_reason" => "end_turn",
#     "usage" => {"input_tokens" => 18, "output_tokens" => 25, ...}}

RubyLLM's stock Anthropic protocol drives it unchanged apart from the request path. LM Studio wants no credentials and no anthropic-version header.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
• Plain exchanges
  • Streaming, with proper message_start / content_block_delta SSE events
  • Tool calls: tool_use blocks with stop_reason: "tool_use", executed as ordinary RubyLLM::Tool objects in your process
  • Reasoning: with_thinking(effort: :low) puts Anthropic's thinking request field on the wire, LM Studio honors it, and the reasoning comes back as a thinking content block in response.thinking.text; with_thinking(false) turns it off. Anthropic's usage block carries no reasoning token count, so response.tokens.thinking is nil here. Verified on LM Studio 0.4.26.

docs.title: What doesn't
docs.text:
with_schema is ignored, quietly

LM Studio ignores the schema and nothing raises. The same model and schema, two protocols:

# :chat_completions => {"name": "John", "age": 30}
# :anthropic        => "Understood. John is 30 years old. How can I help..."

Use :chat_completions for structured output.

Embeddings and judgments are unaffected: they always go to their own endpoints.

Example 12_anthropic_protocol.rb shows streaming, tools and the with_schema trap side by side.

docs.title: The Native REST API
docs.text:
LM Studio's own API, in two generations. v0 mirrors the OpenAI shapes and adds telemetry; v1 is a different design, with server-stored conversations and model management. The gem uses both.

Path gotcha

Model management lives under /api/v1/models/, not directly under /api/v1/ — it is POST /api/v1/models/load, not POST /api/v1/load.

docs.title: Inference stats — :native_v0
docs.text:
POST /api/v0/chat/completions is a strict superset of /v1/chat/completions: the same request — streaming, with_tools, with_schema and the request extras all included — and the same choices and usage, but it fills in the stats block that the OpenAI endpoint returns empty, and adds model_info and runtime.

RubyLLM.configure { |config| config.lms_protocol = :native_v0 }

response = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms).ask('Hello')
response.raw.body['stats']
# => {"tokens_per_second" => 115.19, "time_to_first_token" => 0.0157,
#     "generation_time" => 0.172, "stop_reason" => "eosFound"}
response.raw.body['runtime']['name']  # => "llama.cpp-mac-arm64-apple-metal-advsimd"

RubyLLM has no field for any of this, so it arrives through Message#raw. Everything else behaves identically: this is the default protocol pointed at a different URL. Reach for it when you want telemetry and the full Chat Completions feature set.

/v1/chat/completions returns a stats key of its own, but it is {} on an ordinary request; it carries draft-token counts only when the model was loaded with a draft_model. The timing figures, model_info and runtime are v0-only.

docs.title: Stateful chat — :native_chat
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/chat offers capabilities the OpenAI surface cannot express:

chat = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms,
                    protocol: :native_chat, assume_model_exists: true)
response = chat.ask('Hello')
Stateful conversations LM Studio stores each response server-side and continues from a response_id instead of replaying history. Ordinary RubyLLM multi-turn chats just work: each request sends only the new messages and points previous_response_id at the last stored response. The id is on response.raw.body['response_id'] and on response.raw_content, which RubyLLM persists — so a chat reloaded from the database (Rails acts_as_chat) continues where it left off. Performance stats response.raw.body['stats'] carries tokens per second, time to first token and token counts; response.tokens (input, output, thinking) is filled from it. Reasoning control chat.with_thinking maps onto the native reasoning setting. RubyLLM's :none effort is sent as LM Studio's off. Reasoning comes back as response.thinking.text, streamed as thinking chunks. See Reasoning. Server-side MCP tools with_provider_options(integrations: [...]) has the server itself run MCP plugins from mcp.json ({ id: 'mcp/playwright' }) or ephemeral MCP servers declared in the request (server_label / server_url), with optional allowed_tools filtering. Executed tool calls appear in response.raw.body['output']. Per-request context length with_provider_options(context_length: 8192). Opting out of storage with_provider_options(store: false) keeps the conversation off the server. The chat is then single-turn: a second ask raises, because the endpoint cannot replay history and has nothing stored to continue from. Sampling settings top_p, top_k, min_p and repeat_penalty are part of the native schema, so with_provider_options(top_k: 40) works here too.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No client-side tools: with_tools raises. Use :chat_completions, or MCP integrations.
  • No structured output: with_schema raises.
  • Image input only as data_url parts.
  • Unknown request keys are rejected, so ttl and draft_model raise a BadRequestError here.

The endpoint reports no stop reason of its own. When a generation runs into the max_output_tokens the request asked for, the provider reports finish_reason: :length from the token counts. (Note the spelling: RubyLLM's stock protocols report truncation as :max_tokens.)

docs.title: Model listing and management
docs.text: The native listings enrich provider.list_models, and the v1 management endpoints back the provider's load_model, unload_model and friends. See Models and Model Management.

docs.title: The OpenAI API
docs.text: The surface most code already targets, and the one with the fewest surprises: on Chat Completions, everything RubyLLM can express works.

docs.title: Chat Completions — :chat_completions
docs.text:
The default protocol; nothing to configure. LM Studio honors the usual OpenAI vocabulary on POST /v1/chat/completions: model, messages, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stream, stop, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, logit_bias, seed, tools / tool_choice, and response_format with a json_schema (strict structured output). Vision models accept image content parts.

You reach all of it through RubyLLM's normal API — with_temperature, with_max_output_tokens, with_tools, with_schema, chat.ask(with: 'image.png') — nothing LM Studio-specific required.

Structured output is grammar-constrained

LM Studio builds a grammar from your schema, so the JSON is always structurally valid — even from weights with no tool training. Whether the values make sense is up to the model: gpt-oss models mangle json_schema values on LM Studio, so the specs use a qwen3 model for structured output.

docs.title: Responses — :responses
docs.text:
LM Studio also serves OpenAI's newer Responses API at POST /v1/responses:

RubyLLM.configure { |config| config.lms_protocol = :responses }

Streaming, multi-turn conversations and client-side tools all work.

with_schema does not work here

LM Studio ignores the schema on this endpoint and nothing raises, so you get unconstrained prose where you expected JSON. Use :chat_completions for structured output.

with_thinking works, reasoning text included. That takes this gem's own Responses subclass: OpenAI never returns raw reasoning, only an optional summary, so RubyLLM's stock protocol reads a reasoning item's summary. LM Studio runs the model locally and has nothing to hide, so it returns the reasoning itself in content as reasoning_text (streamed as response.reasoning_text.delta). The provider reads both shapes.

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text:
Embeddings go to POST /v1/embeddings regardless of which chat protocol is in effect — the provider routes them there itself, because that is the only place LM Studio serves them:

RubyLLM.embed('Hello world', model: 'text-embedding-nomic-embed-text-v1.5', provider: :lms)

docs.title: LM Studio request extras
docs.text:
LM Studio accepts request fields that are not part of OpenAI's vocabulary. RubyLLM merges with_provider_options into the payload as-is, so these work on every chat protocol except :native_chat, whose server rejects unknown keys:

Option What it does ttl Idle time-to-live in seconds for the model handling this request. A JIT-loaded model unloads itself after sitting idle that long (default 60 minutes; each request resets the timer). draft_model Speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes tokens the main model verifies, often speeding generation up substantially. Both models must share a tokenizer family. top_k Sample only from the k most likely tokens. min_p Discard tokens below this base probability. repeat_penalty Penalize recently generated tokens to discourage repetition. 
chat = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)
chat.with_provider_options(
  ttl: 300,                        # unload after 5 idle minutes
  draft_model: 'qwen/qwen3-0.6b',  # speculative decoding
  top_k: 40,
  min_p: 0.05,
  repeat_penalty: 1.1
)
chat.ask('Hello')

docs.title: Reasoning
docs.text:
LM Studio honors OpenAI's reasoning_effort on /v1/chat/completions and answers with reasoning_content and a reasoning_tokens count, which RubyLLM reads into Message#thinking and response.tokens.thinking:

chat = RubyLLM.chat(model: 'qwen/qwen3-4b', provider: :lms)
response = chat.with_thinking(effort: :low).ask('What is 2 + 2?')

response.content              # => "4"
response.thinking.text        # => "The user is asking a simple arithmetic question..."
response.tokens.thinking      # => 40

Reasoning works on every chat protocol. On :anthropic it travels as Anthropic's thinking request field and comes back as a thinking content block; see The Anthropic API.

docs.title: What a model supports
docs.text:
chat.with_thinking with no arguments, and chat.with_thinking(false), both resolve against the model registry: the provider reads each model's capabilities.reasoning from LM Studio's native listing and records it as RubyLLM reasoning options, so RubyLLM knows which efforts the model takes and whether it can be switched off at all.

model = RubyLLM.models.find('qwen/qwen3.8-27b', provider: :lms)
model.supports?(:reasoning)                  # => true
model.reasoning_option_values(:effort)       # => ["none", "low", "medium", "xhigh"]

Pass provider: :lms: without it, find searches the whole registry and can return another provider's entry for the same model name, with different reasoning options.

That information comes from the native listing, so it is only in RubyLLM.models for models present in the catalog you registered — see The Packaged Catalog.

A model that reports no way to stop reasoning — gpt-oss lists only low/medium/high — makes with_thinking(false) raise when the request is sent, on ask. That is the registry telling you the truth about the model, not a gap in the catalog.

docs.title: Two vocabularies, translated for you
docs.text:
Accepted values /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses, /api/v0/chat/completions none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh /api/v1/chat (:native_chat) off, low, medium, high, xhigh, on RubyLLM's registry (what Model#reasoning_options reports) the first row, plus a :toggle option where LM Studio offers on

The provider translates LM Studio's off to RubyLLM's none when reading the listing, and back to off when :native_chat sends a request.

docs.title: Models without reasoning
docs.text:
The surfaces differ in how they treat a model that has none. The OpenAI endpoints accept reasoning_effort for any model and silently ignore it; POST /api/v1/chat rejects the request outright:

Model 'bible-study-phi3-mini' does not expose reasoning configuration.

So on :native_chat, only ask for reasoning from a model whose listing reports it. with_thinking and with_thinking(false) refuse before any request is sent (on ask) for a model that reports no reasoning options — one in the registry without them, or one not in your catalog at all. Only an explicit with_thinking(effort:) reaches the server and gets the error above.
